https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.title: Exclusive: Armed Forces shake-up could cut pay of senior officers to reward low-ranking troops
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.subtitle: Forthcoming review will also look into awarding medals to all military personnel who serve overseas to recognise time spent away from family
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.text:
Senior members of the Armed Forces face future pay cuts as part of a comprehensive review into giving lower ranks more money, The Telegraph can disclose.
The review, which will be conducted by external consultants, is expected to report back in 18 months on how to address imbalances between officers and rank and file troops.
It will be announced on Monday as part of the Ministry of Defence’s Command Paper, which was drawn up in tandem with the recently published Integrated Review.
The Telegraph also understands that the review will look into awarding all military personnel who serve overseas Operational Service Medals (OSM), which are currently only given to troops engaged in combat.
The move would serve to recognise the time men and women have served away from family and friends, but may not have been engaged in direct enemy battle, such as the 900 personnel stationed at Tapa Camp as part of Operation Cabrit in Estonia.
Described as “a planned rebalancing of pay within the Armed Forces”, it will attempt to redistribute salary and benefits based on seniority and rank and instead give to military personnel based on contribution on the ground.
As part of the review it is understood that higher ranking personnel will likely see cuts to perks, which include private cars with drivers and more spacious living quarters, which they are given with the view to entertaining people.
Another perk which may be under review is the Continuation of Education Allowance, which gives children of all military personnel the option to attend boarding school if a parent is deployed overseas. However, it is deemed controversial as many junior ranking personnel do not benefit from this as they are unlikely to have families with school age children when deployed overseas.
One Army source said the review was “a rebalancing of the pot so those in the front line and serving overseas get better rewarded”.
They added that it was an attempt to “trim”  a “cohort of military senior people who don't really contribute but get as many allowances as they can”.
Robert Clark, a defence fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, who served as a junior non-commissioned officer in Iraq and Afghanistan, said: “There is a sense in the lower ranks of a growing disparity between those risking their lives on the front lines and those of senior ranks that are entitled to generous perks and allowances
"If this imbalance is addressed it will go some way in improving morale and retention issues.”
However, General Lord Dannatt, the former head of the Army, said he was “horrified” at the suggestion, which he dismissed as the “politics of envy”.
Lord Dannatt said while it was “perfectly acceptable” to have an “allowance of additional pay for those who are away from home for extended periods of time”, it would be “unacceptable” if there was “a reduction in pay for those who were not deployed”.
“I would be horrified if there's any suggestion in cutting pay for those who are at home as their pay is set on a fair basis,” he said.
“The military would also agree that we don't deserve perks, we actually only require those things to enable people to do their job better, or to live their life appropriately.”
One government source said: “Generals won’t like their perks being cut back one jot.”
Although the Government’s Armed Forces’ Pay Review Body Pay was increased by 2 per cent in 2020-21, pay rises for 2021-22 were “paused”, excluding personnel who earn less than £24,000.
Earlier this week Johnny Mercer, the veterans minister, tweeted : “Lots of speculation around the People space in the Defence paper out Monday. Reality: this will be the first with an address specifically to our People in it; outlining why a career in the Military remains amongst the best careers available in the UK today. Exciting and positive.”
An MoD spokesman said: “We always seek to give our personnel the best offer we can throughout their Armed Forces career. “The Defence Secretary will set out further details on Monday and we do not comment on speculation.”

image.caption: A soldier holds an N-LAW light anti-tank weapon on a training exercise on Salisbury Plain for deployment on Operation Cabrit in Estonia

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.title: First meteorite found in UK for 30 years - and extremely rare example - could hold secrets of solar system
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.subtitle: The meteorite could hold secrets of our solar system
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.text:
When a family fast asleep in the Cotswolds were woken by an almighty thud, they could never have known that the object causing it may be the key to finding out how life formed on Earth.
The 300g rock on their driveway which made the noise, was the first meteorite to be found in the UK for 30 years. It landed after zooming through the air as a fireball.
Surveying the strange object outside their home they guessed it was rather special, and summoned scientists from the Natural History Museum to investigate.
They are now studying the meteorite, held at the London facility, which was seen by people on the ground as a fireball lighting up the sky.
The meteorite is an extremely rare type called a carbonaceous chondrite, which have been known to contain organics and amino acids – ingredients for life.
Because of this, it could be a crucial tool in unlocking the secrets to how life began on Earth, and the early history of our solar system.
Researchers are also delighted with its condition, making it ideal to study. Because it was handled so carefully by those who found it, and they alerted scientists so quickly after its fall, it is comparable to the samples returned from space missions, both in quality and quantity.
The family, who do not want to be named, found 300g of the meteorite, which survived its fiery passage through the Earth’s atmosphere and landed on their driveway in the small Cotswold town of Winchcombe.
The fireball sparked hundreds of reports of sightings prompting warnings for the public not to touch meteorite fragments.
Pieces of meteor are believed to have landed in Cheltenham or nearby after the yellow-green fireball was visible for around six seconds at 9.55pm on February 28th.
There have now been more than 900 reports of sightings to the International Meteor Organisation (IMO), which have come from as far away as Belgium and the Netherlands.
Dr Richard Greenwood, Research Fellow in Planetary Sciences at the Open University was the first scientist to identify and advise on the meteorite.
He said: "I was in shock when I saw it and immediately knew it was a rare meteorite and a totally unique event. It’s emotional being the first one to confirm to the people standing in front of you that the thud they heard on their driveway overnight is in fact the real thing."
It is now easier to find meteorites, seen as fireballs in the sky, because of a group of scientists called the UK Fireball Alliance.
They were able to use citizen science videos of the fireball, as well as their own special cameras, to pinpoint the area the meterorite likely landed, and alert the local community to look for fragments.
More meteorite pieces have now been found in the Cotswolds since the driveway discovery.
This meteorite is a rare find; there are approximately 65 thousand known meteorites on Earth. Of these, only 51 of them are carbonaceous chondrites. This is the first known carbonaceous chondrite to have been found in the UK, and the first meteorite recovered in the UK in 30 years. The last meteorite that was discovered in the UK was the Glatton meteorite that landed in a residential garden in 1991.
Over 1,000 meteorites the size of a football are believed to fall to Earth every year, however it is very rare for any of them to be seen to fall and recovered.
Prof Sara Russell, Merit Researcher in Cosmic Mineralogy at the Museum has been tasked with getting the rock analysed before it deteriorates.
She told The Telegraph that the mission was a race against time, explaining: "In the first instance we will send a piece of the meteorite next door, to Imperial College, where the organics will be characterised by mass spectrometry. The carbon and nitrogen isotopes of organic material will be analysed at the Open University also.  It is important these measurements are made quite quickly as the meteorite will be easily terrestrially contaminated. "
Carbonaceous chondrites are known as the most primitive and pristine materials of the solar system and can provide unique information on where water and the building blocks of life were formed and what planets are made from - some of the biggest questions asked by the scientific community.
Dr Luke Daly from the University of Glasgow co-leads the UK Fireball Network.
He said: “It’s thanks to this international collaboration, including researchers as far away as Australia, that we were able to calculate where this meteorite landed so quickly and with such accuracy, as well as where it originated from in the asteroid belt, a rarity that can be said of only about 40 of the 65,000 meteorites on Earth. Goodwill and teamwork have produced a stellar result.”
The team believe that more fragments may yet be discovered, and has urged people in the Cotswolds to keep an eye out for black stones or piles of tiny rocks.
The rocks are incredibly fragile so locals are asked to take a photo of it and record its location, before carefully collecting the sample using a gloved hand or in aluminium foil and contacting the Natural History Museum.

image.caption: Cotswolds meteorite could hold the key to life
The meteorite was seen as a fireball in the sky
The 2cm-wide meteorite fell with a thud on someone's drive in Gloucestershire

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.title: London Fire Brigade should 'face up' to its culture of racism and misogyny, says chief
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.subtitle: Andy Roe said his mixed-race daughter may not be welcome in some fire stations
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03.text:
The London Fire Brigade chief has said his mixed-race daughter may not be welcome in some fire stations, as he called for the organisation to “face up” to its culture of racism and misogyny.
Andy Roe, the London Fire Brigade (LFB) commissioner, this week launched an independent review into its workplace culture and the representation among its workforce.
It comes after an inquest into the death of trainee firefighter, Jaden Francois-Esprit, concluded last month. Mr Francois-Esprit died by suicide in August 2020.
His family were concerned he was being bullied due to his race, adding that he had been mocked about Caribbean food in his packed lunches, the inquest at King’s Cross Coroner’s Court heard.
Coroner Mary Hassell said there was insufficient evidence to link bullying or racism to Mr Francois-Esprit’s death, but raised concerns about his mental health which had gone “undetected by those around him”.
She urged the LFB: “Action should be taken to prevent future deaths and I believe that you have the power to take such action."
“Jaden’s death poses very tough questions for us as an organisation about how we treat young people, how we view difference, how we genuinely make everyone feel welcome,” Mr Roe told The Guardian.
“I don’t need the inquest to show me that race may be an issue – I’ve only got to look at our own data.”
He went on to praise his colleagues who risk their lives regularly and “have reached in to rescue people regardless of background”.
But he added: “In my experience the same people might then come back to the fire station and express themselves casually in racist terms, in misogynist terms, use crude language around faith and sexuality.”
There are still “elements of our culture” that the organisation needs to “transparently face up to and unpick”, he added.
Speaking of his own mixed-heritage family, Mr Roe told The Guardian: “The benchmark for me is I’ve got a young mixed-heritage daughter. Can I say with confidence that she will be treated with dignity and respect in every single part of the London fire brigade? No I can’t.”
“I just want proper change. I want my daughter to walk confidently on to a fire station if she chooses to join in six or seven years’ time, and to feel welcomed and comfortable there,” he added.
The independent review will look at the representation of race, gender and sexual orientation within the LFB, Mr Roe said.

image.caption: Andy Roe was appointed as London's new London Fire Brigade commissioner in 2019, after previous incumbent Dany Cotton resigned in the wake of the Grenfell Tower disaster

author: Lizzie Roberts
